Τῶν κινουμένων τὰ μέν τινα ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἔχει τὴν τῆς κινήσεως αἰτίαν, ἕτερα δὲ ἔξωϑεν μόνον κινεῖται. ἔξωϑεν μὲν οὖν μόνον κινεῖται τὰ φορητά, οἷον ξύλα καὶ λίϑοι καὶ πᾶσα ἡ ὑπὸ ἕξεως μόνης συνεχομένη ὕλη. ὑπεξηῃηρήσϑω δὲ νῦν τοῦ λόγου τὸ κίνησιν λέγειν τὴν δύσιν τῶν σωμάτων, ἐπεὶ μὴ χρεία τούτου πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον. ἐν ξαυτοῖς δὲ ἔχει τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ κινεῖσϑαι ζῷα καὶ φυτὰ καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ὅσα ὑπὸ φύσεως ἢ ψυχῆς συνέχεται: ἐξ ὧν φασιν εἶναι xci τὰ μέταλλα, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις καὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτοκίνητόν ἐστι, τάχα δὲ καὶ αἱ πηγαί. τῶν δὲ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ κινεῖσϑαι ἐχοντῶν τὰ μέν φασιν ἐξ ἑαυτῶν χινεῖσϑαι, τὰ δὲ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν" ἐξ ξαυτῶν μὲν τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα. καὶ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν xiνεῖται τὰ ἔμψυχα, φαντασίας ἐγγινομένης ὁρμὴν προκαλουμένης. xal πάλιν Ev τισι τῶν ζῴων φαντασίαι γίνονται ὁρμὴν προ καλούμεναι, φύσεως φανταστικῆς τεταγμένως κινούσης τὴν ὁρμήν, ος ἐν τῷ ἀράχνῃ φαντασία τοῦ ὑφαίνειν γίνεται καὶ ὁρμὴ ἀκολουϑεῖ ἐπὶ τὸ ὑφαίνειν, τῆς φανταστικῆς αὐτοῦ φύσεως τεταγμένως ἐπὶ τοῦτο αὐτὸν προκαλουμένης xal οὐδενὸς ἄλλου μετὰ τὴν φανταστικὴν αὖτοῦ φύσιν πεπιστευμένου τοῦ ζῴου, καὶ ἐν τῇ μελίσσῃ ἐπὶ τὸ χηροσπλαστεῖν. 3(2). Τὸ μέντοι λογικὸν ζῷον καὶ λόγον ἔχει πρὸς τῇ φανταστικῇ φύσει, τὸν χρίνοντα τὰς φαντασίας καὶ τινὰς μὲν ἀποδοκιμάζοντα τινὰς δὲ παραδεχόμενον, ἵνα ἄγηται τὸ ζῷον κατ᾽ αὐτάς. ὅϑεν ἐπεὶ ἐν τῇ φύσει τοῦ λόγου εἰσὶν ἀφορμαὶ τοῦ ϑεωρῆσαι τὸ καλὸν xai τὸ αἰσχρόν, αἷς ἑπόμενοι ϑεωρήσαντες τὸ καλὸν καὶ τὸ αἰσχρὸν αἱρούμεϑα μὲν τὸ καλὸν ἐκκλίνομεν δὲ τὸ αἰσχρόν, ἐπαινετοὶ μέν ἔσμεν ἐπιδόντες ἑαυτοὺς τῇ πράξει τοῦ καλοῦ, ψεχτοὶ δὲ κατὰ τὸ ἐναντίον. οὐχ ἀγνοητέον μέντοι γε ὅτι τὸ πλέον τῆς εἰς πάντα τεταγμένης φύσεως ποσῶς ἐστιν ἐν τοῖς ζῴοις, ἐπὶ τὸ πλέον δὲ ἢ ἐπὶ τὸ ἔλαττον" ὥστε ἐγγύς που εἶναι, ἵν᾽ οὕτως εἴπω, τοῦ λογικοῦ τὸ ἐν τοῖς ἰχνευταῖς κυσὶν ἔργον xoi ἐν τοῖς πολεμικοῖς ἵπποις. τὸ μὲν οὖν ὑποπεσεῖν τόδε τι τῶν ἔξωϑεν, φαντασίαν ἡμῖν κινοῦν τοιάνδε ἢ τοιάνδε, ὁμολογουμένως οὐκ ἔστι τῶν ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν" τὸ δὲ κρῖναι οὑτωσὶ χρήσασϑαι τῷ γενομένῳ ἢ ἑτέρως, οὐχ ἄλλου τινὸς ἔργον 7 τοῦ Ev ἡμῖν λόγου ἐστίν, ἤτοι παρὰ τὰς ἀφορμὰς ἐνεργοῦντος ἡμᾶς πρὸς τὰς ἐπὶ τὸ καλὸν προχαλουμένας καὶ τὸ καϑῆκον ὁρμάς, n ἐπὶ τὸ ἐναντίον ἐκτρέποντος.
pass_a_gloss: He will say in the ecclesiastical proclamation that the word about the righteous anointing of God is contained, which, being believed to be true, also provokes to living well and fleeing from sin in every way, so that we may understand, having been consoled by the Lord, that we take the most necessary problem. And so that we may understand what the self-moved is, it is necessary to unfold the notion of it, so that with it having been clarified, what is being sought may be presented clearly. For of the things being moved, some have the cause of the movement in themselves, but others are moved only from outside. Therefore, the things being carried are moved only from outside, such as wood and stones and all matter that is held together by habit alone. But let the movement of bodies be set aside from the discussion now, since there is no need of this for the present subject. And animals and plants and all things that are held together by nature or soul have the cause of being moved in themselves: from which they say metals are, and besides these, fire is self-moved, and perhaps also springs. And of the things having the cause of being moved in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, but others from outside themselves: from outside themselves, indeed, the non-living things, but from themselves, the living things. And the living things are moved from themselves, a fantasy occurring, an impulse being provoked. And again, in some of the animals, fantasies occur, an impulse being provoked, nature moving the impulse in an orderly way, as in the spider, a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, the imaginative nature of the spider moving it in an orderly way to this very thing, and no other thing being believed by the animal after its imaginative nature, and in the bee, to shape wax. But the rational animal also has reason in relation to its imaginative nature, approving the fantasies and rejecting some, but accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Whence, since in the nature of reason there are starting-points for contemplating the good and the bad, by following which, having contemplated the good and the bad, we choose the good and turn away from the bad, we are praiseworthy, having given ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy, according to the opposite. But it must not be unknown that the greater part of nature that has been ordered to all things is in the animals, and for the most part, or for the lesser part, so that it is near, as it were, to the rational work in the tracking dogs and in the war horses. For the thing that is subjected to this or that from outside, a fantasy moving us in such and such a way, is admittedly not in our power: but to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or otherwise, is the work of no other than our reason, either working in us according to the starting-points that provoke us to the good and to duty, or turning us away to the opposite.
pass_b_english: He will say that the ecclesiastical proclamation contains the word about God's righteous anointing, and that this word—once believed to be true—also provokes us to live well and to flee sin in every way. Through it, once we have been consoled by the Lord, we may grasp the most necessary problem. In order to understand what the self-moved is, we must unfold its concept; once that concept is clarified, what we are seeking can be presented clearly.

Of the things that are moved, some have the cause of their movement within themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Therefore, objects that are carried—such as wood, stones, and all matter held together by habit alone—are moved only from outside. Let the notion of the movement of bodies be set aside from the discussion for now, since it is not needed for the present subject. Animals, plants, and all things held together by nature or soul have the cause of being moved within themselves. From this group, they say metals come; besides these, fire is self-moved, and perhaps springs as well. Among the things that have the cause of being moved within themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from outside themselves. The non-living things are moved from outside themselves; the living things are moved from themselves. Living things are moved from themselves when a fantasy occurs that provokes an impulse. Again, in some animals fantasies occur that provoke an impulse, with nature moving the impulse in an orderly way. For example, in the spider a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, the spider's imaginative nature moving it in an orderly way to this very thing, with no other thing being believed by the animal after its imaginative nature; and in the bee, the impulse is to shape wax.

The rational animal, however, also has reason alongside its imaginative nature—reason that judges the fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Since in the nature of reason there are starting-points for contemplating the good and the bad, by following these we contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good, and turn away from the bad. In doing so we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy when we do the opposite. It must not be overlooked, however, that the greater part of the nature ordered toward all things exists in animals, whether to a greater or a lesser degree, so that it comes near—as it were—to the rational work found in tracking dogs and war horses. To be subjected to this or that external thing, a fantasy moving us in such and such a way, is admittedly not in our power. But to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or otherwise is the work of nothing other than the reason within us—either operating in us according to the starting-points that provoke us toward the good and toward duty, or turning us away toward the opposite.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, particularly the distinction between 'αὐτεξούσιον' (self-moved/power of self-determination) and the mechanical movement of objects. Pass A preserves the complex clauses regarding the spider and bee, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate rendering of the philosophical argument regarding the rational animal and the role of reason in judging impulses.
